goal.statement: Bake a sourdough loaf with an open crumb, and diagnose it when it comes out dense.
goal.audience: someone who has baked with yeast but never with a starter

capstone.prompt: Bake a loaf. If the crumb comes out tight, say which stage caused it and what you would change next time.
rubric: names the stage, not just the symptom

kcs.label: Feed a starter and tell when it is at peak
misconceptions: a starter is ready whenever it has bubbles
a starter that has collapsed is dead

check.stem: Your starter rose, domed, and has just begun to sink. It is…
options: just past peak — usable, but ferment will run faster
dead and needs replacing
not ready, wait for more bubbles
ready only once it stops moving
distractorSource: a starter that has collapsed is dead
a starter is ready whenever it has bubbles
a starter is ready whenever it has bubbles

kcs.label: Mix flour and water and let it hydrate before adding starter
misconceptions: everything should go in at once

check.stem: Why hold back the starter and salt at first?
options: the flour hydrates and gluten starts forming without fermentation running
it makes the dough rise faster
it is only tradition
salt would not dissolve otherwise
distractorSource: everything should go in at once
everything should go in at once
longer autolyse is always better

kcs.label: Judge bulk fermentation by how the dough behaves, not by the clock
misconceptions: a recipe's timing works in any kitchen
doubling in size is the target for bulk

check.stem: The recipe says four hours. Your kitchen is 28°C. You should…
options: watch the dough — it will be ready well before four hours
follow the four hours as written
add an hour to be safe
refrigerate until four hours have passed
distractorSource: a recipe's timing works in any kitchen
a recipe's timing works in any kitchen
doubling in size is the target for bulk

kcs.label: Build strength with folds instead of kneading
misconceptions: more folding always means more structure
folding is a substitute for fermentation

options: once the dough holds its shape and feels airy
after a fixed number of folds regardless
when it stops being sticky
never — keep folding until shaping
distractorSource: more folding always means more structure
folding is a substitute for fermentation
more folding always means more structure

kcs.label: Shape with enough tension to hold a rise
misconceptions: degassing completely is required before shaping

check.stem: What are you trying to achieve when shaping?
options: a taut skin, with the gas inside largely kept
to press out every bubble first
the tightest ball you can manage
a flat disc that will spread in the oven
distractorSource: degassing completely is required before shaping
tighter shaping is always better
tighter shaping is always better

kcs.label: Tell an under-proved loaf from an over-proved one by the poke test
misconceptions: a dough that springs back fast is ready
over-proved and under-proved look the same from outside

check.stem: You poke it and the dent springs back immediately. The dough is…
options: under-proved — give it longer
ready to bake
over-proved — bake at once
ruined
distractorSource: a dough that springs back fast is ready
over-proved and under-proved look the same from outside
over-proved and under-proved look the same from outside

kcs.label: Bake with steam first, then dry heat
misconceptions: steam matters for the whole bake
a hotter oven always gives more rise

check.stem: Why lift the lid partway through?
options: the crust needs to dry and colour once the rise is done
to check on it
to let the loaf cool a little
steam is only needed at the end
distractorSource: steam matters for the whole bake
a hotter oven always gives more rise
steam matters for the whole bake

kcs.label: Read the finished crumb backwards to the stage that caused it
misconceptions: a dense crumb always means the starter was weak
crumb problems are fixed by changing the recipe rather than the timing

check.stem: Tight crumb, pale crust, and it spread flat on the tray. The likeliest cause is…
options: over-fermented — the structure gave out before the bake
under-fermented — it needed longer in bulk
the oven was too cool
the flour was wrong
distractorSource: a dense crumb always means the starter was weak
crumb problems are fixed by changing the recipe rather than the timing
a dense crumb always means the starter was weak
